tldr: In autonomous humanoid boxing, directly exploring raw joint commands leads to balance collapse and falling. This work solves that dilemma by playing a self-play game over a bounded latent motion space learned via motion tracking. It achieves intense punch exchanges and stable footwork between two real Unitree G1 humanoids.
hero_caption: Overall pipeline of RoboStriker. Training proceeds stage by stage: professional boxing motion tracking (Stage I), distillation into a bounded latent space (Stage II), behavioral warm-up (Stage IIIa), and latent-space neural fictitious self-play (LS-NFSP, Stage IIIb).
overview:
In recent years, humanoid locomotion and acrobatic motion tracking have advanced dramatically. However, contact-rich competitive tasks against an opponent, such as boxing, face an entirely different and formidable obstacle.

That obstacle is the fundamental conflict between strategic exploration and physical stability. Finding effective tactics via multi-agent reinforcement learning requires aggressive exploration. But when exploring blindly across a humanoid's 29 raw motor degrees of freedom, joint configurations collapse into falls long before any viable tactics can emerge. With unpredictable impact forces from opponent strikes added to the mix, training breaks down before the robot can even master basic balance.

To overcome this, the authors formulate the competitive task as a two-player zero-sum Markov game over a bounded latent space. First, a pretrained motion decoder creates a compact latent manifold that generates only safe, human-like behaviors. They then introduce RoboStriker, a hierarchical framework where high-level tactical reasoning takes place entirely within this latent space.

In extensive simulation battles using the Unitree G1, RoboStriker decisively outperformed conventional methods exploring raw joint spaces as well as naive self-play baselines, achieving superior win rates and striking efficiency. Furthermore, combat policies trained in simulation were directly deployed onto two real-world Unitree G1 humanoids, demonstrating dynamic boxing exchanges with hard punches and no catastrophic balance failures.
contributions: Formulated competitive humanoid boxing as a two-player zero-sum Markov game over a bounded latent space induced by a pretrained decoder, theoretically analyzing it through an approximate-Nash equilibrium framework.

Proposed RoboStriker, a hierarchical framework that decouples high-level strategic reasoning from low-level execution and prevents policy cycling through Latent-Space Neural Fictitious Self-Play (LS-NFSP) for co-evolution.
Substantially mitigated the cold-start problem and non-stationarity in the early stages of competitive learning by introducing an Adversarial Motion Prior (AMP)-guided behavioral warm-up.
Successfully demonstrated autonomous combat and physical contact behaviors on two 29-DoF Unitree G1 humanoids, both in simulation and on real-world hardware.

sections.heading: Introduction: Why Teaching Humanoids to Box Is So Hard
sections.summary: As humanoid control shifts from single-agent motion tracking to competitive interactions against opponents, the trade-off between strategic exploration and fall prevention becomes the primary roadblock. RoboStriker addresses this with a hierarchical framework that solves games over a bounded latent space.
sections.details:
Humanoid robots have emerged as a premier frontier in Embodied AI. While agile locomotion and acrobatic skills have advanced recently, most works remain confined to single-agent whole-body tracking in static, predictable environments. Extending this to competitive tasks like boxing escalates the challenge from isolated trajectory tracking to mutual adaptation under brutal physical constraints.

The core difficulty lies in the conflict between the flexibility required for strategic interaction and strict physical feasibility. Humanoids like the Unitree G1 possess high-dimensional, unstructured joint spaces where the vast majority of joint combinations represent physically unviable postures. While reinforcement learning demands bold exploration to discover viable tactics, doing so in a fragile, raw action space causes the robot to lose balance and fall long before meaningful combat behaviors emerge.

Constantly receiving falling penalties leads to a physical cold-start problem where the robot cannot even discover a single effective move. Moreover, because the opponent delivers unpredictable strikes, policies operating directly in raw joint space cannot withstand the impacts, causing training to collapse entirely.

To break this bottleneck, the authors formulate boxing as a two-player latent-space zero-sum Markov game. By restricting the exploration space to a bounded manifold via a pretrained low-level motion decoder, high-level decisions take place within this latent space. This eliminates the catastrophic balance failures seen in baselines and allows advanced tactical intelligence to emerge.

sections.heading: Related Work: The Intersection of Motion Tracking, Latent Spaces, and Multi-Agent RL
sections.summary: This section surveys prior work across whole-body motion tracking, latent motion representations, and multi-agent competitive learning. RoboStriker distinguishes itself by repurposing the latent space directly as the strategic action space for competitive games.
sections.details:
This work builds upon three main lines of prior research:

- Humanoid Motion Generation and Control
Physics-based motion imitation has evolved from tracking single trajectories to Adversarial Motion Priors (AMP) and general-purpose motion trackers. However, existing methods focus mostly on single-agent setups tracking externally provided reference trajectories. They cannot be directly applied to competitive interactions that require continuous adaptation to an opponent.

- Latent Motion Representations and Motion Priors
To make high-dimensional motor control tractable, approaches like ASE, CALM, and PULSE embed motion tracking into latent spaces. Rather than merely treating latent spaces as behavior representations, this work uniquely adopts the bounded latent interface as the strategic action space for multi-agent competitive games.

- Competitive Character Control and Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL)
Self-Play and Neural Fictitious Self-Play (NFSP) are well-known frameworks for learning cooperation and competition while preventing strategy cycling. Past works typically applied them directly to raw joint spaces or simplistic physics setups, leading to physical breakdown on complex humanoids. RoboStriker executes NFSP over a compact latent manifold, achieving complete decoupling between low-level whole-body control and high-level combat tactics.

sections.heading: RoboStriker: Constructing Strategic Games in Latent Space
sections.summary: Boxing is formulated as a latent-space zero-sum Markov game solved through a three-stage pipeline: tracking policy learning, topological latent distillation, and fictitious self-play. Constraining the latent space to a bounded hypersphere alongside AMP regularization enables stable, non-collapsing strategic learning.
sections.details:
RoboStriker's training process comprises an elegant theoretical foundation and three sequential stages:

### III-A Two-Player Latent-Space Zero-Sum Markov Game
Let the players be $\mathcal{I}=\{1,2\}$ and the state space be $\mathcal{S}$. In addition to the raw 29-DoF joint position command space $\mathcal{A}^i \subset \mathbb{R}^{29}$, a bounded continuous latent strategy space $\mathcal{Z}^i \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ is defined. A shared pretrained decoder $D_\psi(s, z^i)$ maps latent actions to raw joint commands. This induces environment transitions and utility functions directly over the latent space, establishing a game between latent policies $\pi^i_z$. By iteratively computing bounded-error best responses against the opponent's empirical policy, the co-evolution dynamics can be interpreted as converging to an $\epsilon$-Nash equilibrium in the latent game.

### III-B Expert Motion Tracker Training (Stage I)
Approximately 30 minutes of striking, defending, and footwork data captured from a professional boxer using an Xsens suit at 50 Hz are retargeted to the Unitree G1 skeleton to create $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{motion}}$. The tracker policy $\pi_{\mathrm{trk}}$ takes proprioception $s_t^{\mathrm{prop}}$ and reference poses from the next three future steps $s_t^{\mathrm{ref}}$ as inputs, outputting target joint positions. It is trained with a reward combining pose, orientation, and velocity matching with torque change penalties.

### III-C Motion Encoding via Topological Latent Distillation (Stage II)
To distill tracker capabilities into a compact latent space $\mathcal{Z}$, teacher-student distillation is performed. An encoder $E_\phi$ outputs a latent code $z_t$ from observations, while decoder $D_\psi$ reconstructs teacher actions from current state $s_t^{\mathrm{prop}}$ and $z_t$. Crucially, a prior network $P_\xi(z_t \mid s_t^{\mathrm{prop}})$ predicts the reachable latent distribution from the current state, and KL divergence regularization prevents posterior collapse. Furthermore, latent codes are normalized onto a unit hypersphere, enforcing topological boundedness.

### III-D Behavioral Warm-Up with Adversarial Priors (Stage IIIa)
Starting self-play immediately from scratch leads to poor exploration and stagnation. Therefore, a warm-up phase is introduced where the agent learns to strike a static upright dummy. A residual policy $\pi_\theta$ outputs a residual $\Delta z_t$ relative to the action prior $P^\perp_\xi$. To prevent motion degradation, an AMP discriminator $C$ runs concurrently, providing a style reward $r_{\mathrm{style}}$ for natural movements indistinguishable from reference data.

### III-E Latent-Space Neural Fictitious Self-Play (Stage IIIb: LS-NFSP)
After warm-up, agents proceed to self-play within the latent space. Each agent updates a best-response policy $\pi^{RL}_z$ using PPO on a reinforcement learning buffer $\mathcal{D}_{RL}$, while simultaneously training an average policy $\bar{\pi}_z$ via supervised learning on a reservoir buffer $\mathcal{D}_{SL}$ containing historical strategies. During rollouts, actions are sampled from a mixture strategy blending both policies with mixing parameter $\eta=0.1$. This suppresses rock-paper-scissors policy cycling and ensures stable convergence toward an equilibrium strategy.

sections.heading: Experiments: From Simulation Battles to Real-World Bouts
sections.summary: Using Isaac Lab with 4,096 parallel environments, Unitree G1 humanoids were trained and evaluated against baseline methods, raw action spaces, ablations, and in real-world deployments. RoboStriker achieved outstanding win rates and striking accuracy, proving its balance stability even on physical robots.
sections.details:
Simulations were conducted in Isaac Lab, running 4,096 parallel environments on a single NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU. Physics ran at 200 Hz, while control policies operated at 50 Hz. The latent space dimension was set to 32.

### IV-A & IV-B Evaluation Metrics and Baselines
Baselines included Naive SP (always playing against the latest checkpoint), Fictitious SP (uniformly sampling from historical checkpoints), PPO-Only (playing against a fixed opponent), and 29-DoF Action-Space baselines trained in raw joint space (with and without AMP). Evaluations measured win rate (KO assigned when any part other than the feet touches the ground), effective striking rate ($\eta_{\mathrm{hit}}$: contact force $\ge$ 10 N), engagement ratio (ER: fraction of time maintaining effective distance and facing the opponent), base of support stability (BOS), and torque smoothness ($TS_\tau$).

### IV-C & IV-D Strategic Superiority and Latent Space Impact
RoboStriker achieved near-complete dominance, winning 68.52% against Fictitious SP, 76.24% against Naive SP, and 84.47% against PPO-Only. It also achieved top marks in engagement ratio (0.824) and striking efficiency (0.685). In contrast, the baseline exploring raw 29-DoF space with AMP (29-DoF + AMP) only managed $\eta_{\mathrm{hit}}/ER = 0.285/0.465$, and RoboStriker swept head-to-head matches against it with a 92.50% win rate. This proves that merely regularizing style via AMP is insufficient; structuring the exploration space with a pretrained decoder is vital.

### IV-E Real-Robot Deployment
Policies trained with domain randomization over contact friction and center of mass were deployed at 50 Hz on the onboard CPUs of two Unitree G1 robots via ONNX Runtime. An external motion capture system tracked pelvis positions at 100 Hz to provide relative opponent states. As shown in Figure F3, both physical robots exchanged hard-hitting punches while actively stepping and defending without losing balance or falling.

### IV-F Ablation Studies
Removing AMP caused agents to drop their guards, rush blindly in unnatural postures, and suffer a sharp drop in striking efficiency (Figure F4). Skipping behavioral warm-up caused learning to stall near zero due to sparse rewards. In latent dimension tests, 16 dimensions lacked expressive power (higher MPKPE error), while 64 dimensions introduced redundancy, dropping striking efficiency to 0.520. A 32-dimensional latent space offered the ideal balance.

sections.heading: Conclusion: Toward Merging Embodiment and Strategic Intelligence
sections.summary: By constraining strategic interaction to a bounded latent space and cleanly separating it from low-level execution, RoboStriker resolves the trade-off between physical balance and exploration in humanoid boxing. Supported by theoretical grounding and physical hardware demonstrations, it showcases a viable path to autonomous combat intelligence.
sections.details:
This work provides a clear answer to a deep conflict: balancing strategic exploration in multi-agent reinforcement learning against the inherent physical fragility of humanoid robots.

Formulating competitive interaction as a two-player zero-sum Markov game over a decoder-induced bounded latent space provides not only an approximate-Nash theoretical framework, but also a robust foundation that lets robots evolve sophisticated tactics without catastrophic falls.

Through rigorous baseline evaluations and ablations in simulation, as well as real-world bouts between physical Unitree G1 robots, RoboStriker demonstrated its effectiveness. Looking ahead, this approach holds promise beyond boxing, extending to diverse humanoid tasks requiring high-impact physical interaction and mutual coordination.

takeaways: In competitive interactions for high-DoF robots, learning high-level strategies through a bounded latent motion space (e.g., a unit hypersphere) rather than directly exploring raw joint space is the decisive factor in preventing physical collapse.

Style regularization via Adversarial Motion Priors (AMP) alone is not enough; structuring the exploration space itself with a latent manifold is critical for achieving high tactical performance (striking efficiency and engagement ratio).
Because self-play from scratch is prone to cold-start failures and non-stationarity, incorporating a task-oriented behavioral warm-up against a static dummy is remarkably effective.
Bringing the Neural Fictitious Self-Play (NFSP) framework into the latent space prevents policy cycling (rock-paper-scissors loops) and enables stable strategic co-evolution.
limitations: Real-world robot experiments depend on an external motion capture system (100 Hz) to track the opponent's relative position, falling short of fully autonomous onboard vision-based combat.
The boxing repertoire is bounded by the ~30-minute motion capture dataset collected in Stage I.
Recovery capabilities remain limited when subjected to severe, trip-inducing external disturbances, such as exceptionally hard impacts or unexpected leg sweeps.
